title: The Cracks in Cracking the Alphabetic Code Overstepping Boundaries
author: Janetos, Harriett
summary: The science of learning isn't about prescriptions, it's about probabilities. And this is where knowing the boundary conditions of any principle matters so much. Knowing when not to use it can be as important as knowing when to . . . A principle applied everywhere becomes dogma; a principle applied within its limits increases the probability of it being effective, because it honours the conditions that make it work in the first place. Carl Hendrick, The Learning Dispatch Principles, Not Prescriptions The alphabetic principle organizes beginning reading instruction by explaining how phonemes are represented by graphemes, which leads to clear implications for instruction: teach how to encode phonemes to write and how to decode graphemes to read. Without knowing the necessary constraints on the conditions of learning this principle, we might not realize when we've overstepped essential boundaries--failing to fashion our lessons to conform to these constraints by honoring those conditions that make it work in the first place. However, sometimes these conditions aren't crystal clear. In the field of nutrition, substances can be labeled GRAS: Generally Recognized as Safe. This means there is general agreement among experts based on the available research but no definitive research-based designation about safety. I'm applying GRAS to reading instruction with one distinct difference: Generally Recognized as Successful. This new designation is the topic of this post: how letter knowledge should be taught to honor the conditions of the alphabetic principle and successfully teach students to read. It is generally recognized as successful that letter names and sounds should be taught together because the research generally shows this simultaneous instruction leads to acquiring letter knowledge. However, if my goal is accelerating the reading process--and not just the letter-learning process--then this shift in thinking should shift my instructional focus. A classroom lethal mutation happens when the visible form of a technique survives, but the learning mechanism that made it useful disappears. Haili Hughes, Lethal Mutations in the Classroom [ 1147770&utm_medium=email% 2Cemail&isFreemail=true&comments=true&utm_campaign=email-half-magic-com ments&r=5spuf ] Emphasizing letter sounds during beginning reading instruction and relegating references to letter names for uses not related to teaching students how to segment phonemes (encode) and blend graphemes (decode), neither one of which requires using letter names, does deviate from this GRAS recommendation. But does this deviation diminish the ability to learn and apply reading skills to accomplish these two essential processes? I may be taking liberties with Carl Hendrick's statement about the importance of knowing the boundary conditions of a principle, but applying it to the alphabetic principle does aid my decision-making. If this principle--how phonemes are represented by graphemes--sets our boundary conditions of teaching letter knowledge, then staying inside this boundary until my students have understood this principle and can apply it independently may, in fact, be the best instructional decision I can make. At least that's what I've been betting on. You Say Letter Names, I Say Letter Sounds I make the choice to teach letter sounds before letter names to help beginning readers focus immediately and intently on mastering the alphabetic principle. Since decoding requires children to connect graphemes to phonemes, emphasizing sounds first may reduce the confusion that can arise when children try to use letter names while blending words, which I have experienced in my intervention sessions. Prioritizing sounds can therefore streamline early decoding by directing attention to the functional role letter sounds play in reading words. Of course, letter names matter in other areas and are eventually essential for spelling and labeling, but introducing sounds first during reading instruction may provide a clearer and more direct route into word reading for many novice learners. I witnessed this letter-name confusion soon after getting my reading specialist credential. I asked a third grader to read the word play. He proclaimed that was easy and proceeded to say: P-l-a-y--play. However when I asked him to read the word gray, he said gr--een. He had memorized the spelling of the word play but had not orthographically mapped the spelling pattern ay by matching the phoneme to the grapheme, so he merely guessed after the first two letters when reading gray. More commonly, an emphasis on sounds prevents getting a Halloween story about a yitch and writing the word when as yn. With the exception of the vowels, letter names are syllables--not phonemes--which undermines the direct application of letter-sound knowledge necessary for decoding and encoding words because it crosses our boundary conditions that are set by the role of the phoneme in beginning reading instruction. Recently, I wrote about Mark Seidenberg's concerns that we are overteaching phonics. What I didn't mention in the comments section of his blog, nor in my own blog, is that the general consensus among researchers who recommend teaching letter sounds and names together might itself be a good example of overteaching letter knowledge at the beginning and therefore unnecessary overreach when it comes to establishing foundational skills. I am very familiar with the argument that letter names are useful labels and how they can facilitate learning sounds. However, I am not convinced based on my years of experience teaching K-1 students in the classroom--and also working with hundreds of reading intervention students--that teaching letter names is essential at the very beginning. In fact, I ask why the opposite can't also be true: Can't letter-sound knowledge be used to facilitate letter-name knowledge? It appears I am in good company with this stance based on a new study about the 100-year-old Montessori method, which prioritizes letter sounds over letter names. In fact, right before teaching kindergarten, I visited the local Montessori school to observe lessons and discuss their approach to reading. I was persuaded by the logic behind their instructional choices and applied their emphasis on letter sounds in my classroom. Cutting out the middleman--letter names--simplified both my reading and writing instruction by focusing on the phonemes used when encoding and decoding. I did refer to letter names in other situations--like the A-Z levels in the school's online reading program--but I kept reading instruction time sound-centric, respecting what I considered to be the boundary conditions of the alphabetic principle within these processes. Montessori Makes It Work The Montessori method has received this positive publicity recently due to research showing reading gains by the end of kindergarten for those students who received Montessori training in preschool. I cite this study simply to point out that if evidence for letter-name instruction specifically geared to reading outcomes is not conclusive--indicating in many instances correlation rather than causation--we can take other factors into consideration in order to make our curricular choices. Here are some examples of the counterargument: From This 100-year-old teaching method is beating modern preschools : A first-of-its-kind national trial shows that public Montessori preschool students enter kindergarten with stronger reading, memory, and executive function skills than their peers. These gains don't fade -- they grow over time, bucking a long-standing trend in early education research. From How Montessori Teaches the Alphabet and Phonics : In Montessori, the alphabet is taught out of order and with the sounds the letters make before teaching the names of the letters. It is typically taught in 6 different sets of letters. This helps children learn to read better because they associate the correct sounds with letters. The Montessori way of teaching the alphabet provides many benefits that the traditional way of teaching does not offer. The more you understand about this way of teaching children, the more it makes sense. From Episode 11 of Sold a Story, which profiles the Success for All program in Steubenville, Ohio: The kids are saying the sounds of the letters. But they're not saying the names of the letters. This is a particular way of teaching letters. It's sometimes referred to as the "sounds first" approach. And it's not the way letters are typically taught in American schools. Typically, kids are taught the names of letters first . . . You need to know the names of letters and the order of the alphabet to be a literate person. But what do you need to know to learn how to read? To learn how to read, you don't need to know the names of the letters. In fact, the letter names can be confusing. For example, the most common sound of the letter "e" in English is not "ee." It's "eh." As in "bed" and "fed." And the most common sound of the letter "i" is not "eye." It's "/i/" as in "sit" and "pin." The idea in a "sounds first" approach is to focus children's attention on the sounds of letters. So when they're trying to read a word, the sounds are what immediately come to mind. There's no interference, no confusion with the names of the letters . . . There's actually some disagreement among cognitive scientists about whether it's better to start with the letter names or the letter sounds. The bottom line is that kids need to learn both. And it's not that kids in Steubenville aren't taught the names of letters -- they are. It's just that there's an emphasis on letter sounds to try to reduce clutter, to minimize the chances that a child will be confused. In other words, there's an emphasis on how children learn. And what might be difficult for a beginner. Children Learn What They Are Taught In addition to visiting the local Montessori school prior to teaching kindergarten, I looked at research on the letter sound vs. letter name controversy, including that by Rebecca Treiman (Instruction Matters: Spelling of Vowels by Children in England and the US , Reading and Writing, 2013) that found no significant differences in outcomes between English children who received letter-sound instruction and American Children who had an emphasis on letter-names, validating Diane McGuinness's assertion that children learn what they are taught. U.K. literacy educator and contributor to the post-Rose Report reading program Letters and Sounds recounts her own experiences with names and sounds: I loved stories and was longing to learn how to translate those black marks into spoken words so that I could read stories to myself. When I started school, we sang an alphabet song every morning, but when it came to reading and spelling lessons, the emphasis was all on letter-sounds, and it made so much sense that I made up my own private version of the alphabet song using letter-sounds rather than letter-names. More support for emphasizing sounds over names: From developmental psychologist D.B. Elkonin, in Comparative Reading: Cross-National Studies of Behavior and Processes in Reading and Writing, (1973): When children of six to seven years already know the names of many letters before they can read, they'll try to simply put together the names of letters . . . one of the worst habits with which many children enter school . . . and it is necessary to teach them afresh. From cognitive psychologist Diane McGuinness, In Early Reading Instruction: What Science Really Tells Us About How to Teach Reading, 2004: Letter names are something a child has to unlearn to be able to read . . . Letter names mislead children in two ways: by directing attention to the wrong phonological unit [the syllable] for the writing system, and by causing them to misrepresent the sound-to-print correspondences. From neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene in Reading in the Brain, 2009: The goal of reading becomes very clear. It must aim to lay down an efficient neuronal hierarchy, so that a child can recognize letters and graphemes and easily turn them into speech sounds . . . Considerable research . . . converges on the fact that grapheme-phoneme conversion radically transforms the child's brain and the way in which it processes speech sounds . . . The names of letters . . . far from being helpful, may even delay the acquisition of reading . . . Letter names cannot be assembled during reading--the hookup only concerns phonemes. For me, accepting the boundary conditions of the alphabetic principle was not constraining. In fact, it was liberating because it narrowed my instructional choices, which helped focus my lessons and simplify my instruction. While I continue to read the research by Shayne Piasta and others who recommend simultaneous instruction in sounds and names, I am also encouraged by studies like this one: The finding that teaching letter sounds first benefited both accurate and rapid letter sound learning overall for both DLL and non-DLL children recommends teaching letter sounds first. Roberts, T. A., Vadasy, P. F. & Sanders, E. A. (2019). Preschoolers' alphabet learning: Cognitive teaching sequence, and English proficiency influences. Reading Research Quarterly Call it confirmation bias or a call to action, but this study has motivated me to continue prioritizing sounds over names during beginning reading instruction simply because I want to maximize every opportunity I have to emphasize the importance of the alphabetic principle, which matches sounds--not names--to letters. And yes--I really have had students who really do try to blend words using letter names (em-ay-tee) instead of letter sounds: /m/ /a/ /t/. Over the past two decades I have had a schedule that combines working with intervention students while also doing job shares in grades K-4. The latter afforded me the opportunity to work with striving students within the context of a whole-class setting in addition to seeing some of these students in my small group intervention sessions. This familiarity with the challenges these students face has translated into the urgency I feel to facilitate reading grade-level text as quickly as possible. If I can cut corners without compromising the learning process, I will do so every time. Recommendation Rubbernecking It can be frustrating watching reading recommendations over the years bounce between sidelining and supercharging phonics, especially considering the opportunity costs for every instructional choice we make. We need to look at the available research and examine each and every recommendation by asking: What are the non-negotiables when it comes to teaching foundational skills? How do we decide what, when, how, and how much to teach--and to whom? What are the 'nice-to-knows' vs. the 'need-to-knows'? Where does the preponderance of the evidence related to encoding and decoding lie? How do we prioritize some literacy components without crowding out others? In some respects, even post-balanced literacy, we are still in romance vs. reality territory when it comes to reading instruction. But even within the stark reality of code-based instruction, we sometimes veer into using methods that are unnecessary. Maybe this is an ultra-reality that does not serve the best interests of our students because it runs straight into and counter to best practices in teaching reading. Maybe we need to do a better job establishing the boundary conditions of the principles we are teaching. Maybe Maria Montessori was on to something. It seems inconceivable that we will continue wasting energy on the reading wars simply because we cannot get both sides to say simultaneously, 'some teachers overdo phonics' and 'some students need explicit instruction in alphabetic coding.' Keith Stanovich, Romance and Reality Always striving to make sense--please let me know when I fail. Thanks for reading Making Words Make Sense! Subscribe for free to receive new posts.
